blocks.heading: Profit and cash are different
blocks.text: Profit measures income earned less the relevant costs and expenses over a period; cash is money available and movements of money received or paid. A credit sale can add to profit before the customer pays. Paying for a long-lived asset reduces cash without making its full purchase price an immediate expense in the simple trading-profit calculation. Borrowing increases cash and liabilities rather than profit. Repaying loan principal reduces cash and liabilities rather than being an ordinary trading expense, whereas interest is an expense. Depreciation reduces recorded profit while involving no current cash payment for that depreciation charge. These timing and classification differences explain why a profitable enterprise may struggle to pay bills. Examine receipts, payments and due dates rather than assuming a profit figure is money in the bank.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Teya Cabinets sells a cabinet on credit for N$5,000. The materials and other relevant cost of that sale total N$3,000, already paid. The customer will pay next month. The sale contributes N$2,000 profit before other relevant expenses, but it provides no customer cash yet. The business has already paid N$3,000, so cash timing can be difficult despite a profitable sale. When the debtor pays, cash rises and the amount owed falls; it is not a second sale.

blocks.heading: Keeping the ideas apart
blocks.text:
Explain why a credit sale can increase profit before cash rises. Fictional Hila Repairs earns N$3,000 for completed work with relevant costs N$2,000 already paid, and the customer pays next month.

The work contributes N$1,000 profit under the stated figures, but no customer receipt has yet arrived. The amount owed is a debtor. When payment arrives next month, cash rises and the debtor falls; it does not create the same income again. Profit timing and cash timing are different.
